articles.headline: El Vista Alegre de Burela inicia el curso exigiendo a la Xunta un calendario para su reforma integral
articles.subtitle: El Consello Escolar aprobó por unanimidad remitir un nuevo escrito a la Consellería de Educación, que responde a sus demandas con un informe de agosto de 2025. Son cinco años de reclamaciones y el BNG llevará una moción al próximo pleno municipal.
articles.body:
La comunidad educativa del CEIP Vista Alegre de Burela ha comenzado el nuevo curso igual que acabó el anterior: con protestas y con la exigencia de una rehabilitación integral de un edificio de más de cuatro décadas que, sostienen, arrastra humedades, instalaciones obsoletas y problemas de accesibilidad.

El lunes, el Consello Escolar aprobó por unanimidad registrar un escrito ante la secretaría general técnica de la Consellería de Educación en respuesta al informe remitido por la Administración el 1 de septiembre. La Anpa, que preveía presentarlo este martes, sostiene que esa contestación no responde a la solicitud de información que formuló en agosto.

La asociación censura que se les haya enviado un documento fechado en agosto de 2025, cuando en febrero de este año la dirección y el consejo escolar elaboraron una memoria con las deficiencias del edificio. Preguntan si esa memoria entró en el expediente y por qué el informe ignora necesidades que ella recoge y menciona otras que la Anpa nunca planteó.

Lo que piden es un calendario de actuación definido y una intervención global, no obras sueltas; son cinco años de reclamaciones.

La Xunta ha negado problemas estructurales: su delegado en Lugo, Javier Arias, cifró en unos 75.000 euros las mejoras de los últimos tres años y atribuyó parte del deterioro al mantenimiento del Concello. En junio, el PP rechazó en el Parlamento gallego una proposición del BNG para acometer la reforma.

Este lunes, el teniente de alcalde de Burela, Mario Pillado, anunció que el BNG presentará una moción en el próximo pleno municipal, tras reunirse con la presidenta de la Anpa, el director del Vista Alegre y la del IES Perdouro, que también arrastra problemas de accesibilidad. «Burela ten que deixar de ser discriminada», afirmó.

articles.headline: La jueza de la Audiencia Nacional ve una "gestión favorecedora" desde Marruecos en la avalancha de Ceuta
articles.subtitle: María Tardón se declara competente, respalda el informe policial sobre una entrada "planificada" y ordena investigar también la respuesta de España a las alertas previas. La Fiscalía ya había avalado que asumiera la causa.
articles.body:
La jueza de la Audiencia Nacional María Tardón se declaró este lunes competente para instruir la entrada masiva en Ceuta y avaló el informe policial que sitúa el origen en Marruecos. En un auto de 26 folios sostiene que hubo una gestión "clara e indudable" y "favorecedora del proceso desde el territorio del Reino de Marruecos", con agentes marroquíes guiando activamente a quienes cruzaban la frontera.

La magistrada concluye que la oleada no fue un episodio espontáneo, sino un proceso planificado con al menos cinco niveles, desde los dinamizadores del mensaje hasta actores de dirección aún no identificados, y ve indicios de cuatro delitos, entre ellos contra la paz o la independencia del Estado y en conexión con los 84 fallecidos.

Tardón no se limita a la orilla marroquí: ordena investigar qué se hizo en territorio español ante las alertas previas, en particular la del Centro Nacional de Inmigración y Fronteras del 29 de julio, que avisaba de un "riesgo extremo" de entradas a nado y salto coordinado a la valla. Sánchez e Interior habían restado peso a esos avisos, calificados de "rutinarios".

El Gobierno insiste en que ningún informe identifica un "autor intelectual": el ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, sostuvo este lunes que no existe un elemento "mínimamente lógico, razonable y objetivo" contra Marruecos ni contra ningún otro Estado.

articles.headline: El ex presidente de Plus Ultra confirma ante el juez el pago de una comisión del 1% al entorno de Zapatero
articles.subtitle: Julio Martínez Solá ratificó que la aerolínea abonó unos 530.000 euros para asegurarse el rescate de 53 millones, mientras el juez Calama desestimaba el recurso de Zapatero contra la investigación de sus cuentas y las de sus hijas.
articles.body:
El caso Plus Ultra aceleró este lunes en la Audiencia Nacional. El juez José Luis Calama desestimó el recurso del expresidente del Gobierno José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero contra la autorización a la UDEF para investigar las cuentas bancarias del exmandatario, las de sus hijas y las de su secretaria, todos imputados en la causa por el rescate de 53 millones concedido a la aerolínea en pandemia.

En la misma jornada, el expresidente de Plus Ultra, Julio Martínez Solá, ratificó ante el juez que la compañía aceptó pagar una comisión del 1%, unos 530.000 euros, al "grupo Zapatero" a través de Julio Martínez Martínez, considerado su testaferro, para asegurarse la concesión de la ayuda pública. En los chats intervenidos por la UDEF, los investigados la llamaban "mordida"; se pagó "ante la duda" de que la gestión surtiera efecto y se canalizó a través de tres sociedades.

Juez y fiscal de Anticorrupción quieren determinar además si la aerolínea, controlada en un 64% por capital extranjero, cumplía los requisitos para acceder a las ayudas de la Sepi, y rastrean un posible blanqueo posterior al rescate. Este martes declara el ex consejero delegado Roberto Roselli, que también ha decidido colaborar.

La defensa de Zapatero alegó vulneración de la intimidad y del secreto de las comunicaciones. El juez responde que la actuación policial queda delimitada por el perímetro ya autorizado y que el riesgo de difusión indebida "no es un criterio jurídico para limitar la investigación".

articles.headline: Sánchez pone al PSOE en guardia ante un posible adelanto electoral y arranca el curso a la defensiva
articles.subtitle: El presidente pide a los suyos vaciarse y "echar el resto" sin concretar fecha electoral, mientras un sector del partido lo lee como preparación de unas generales adelantadas al primer trimestre de 2027.
articles.body:
Pedro Sánchez reunió este lunes a los parlamentarios socialistas para abrir el último curso de la legislatura con un mensaje doble: pidió a los suyos "vaciarse" y "echar el resto", y proyectó su ambición más allá del mandato, hasta 2031. "Casi llevamos ocho años y, el año que viene, otros cuatro más", dijo.

La ausencia de fecha no disipó las lecturas: un sector del partido interpreta la llamada al esfuerzo como la preparación de un adelanto electoral para el primer trimestre de 2027, si el Congreso tumba los Presupuestos a final de año. El presidente vinculó el pulso al auge de la ultraderecha en Europa: la victoria de AfD en Sajonia-Anhalt es, dijo, "un aviso" de que "la amenaza ultra gana terreno".

Sánchez citó como prioridades legislativas la reducción de ratios escolares, la protección de menores en entornos digitales, el blindaje del aborto y la ley de integridad pública, y prometió unos presupuestos para 2027 centrados en la vivienda, sin calendario pese a que el plazo constitucional para remitirlos a las Cortes expira en octubre.

Moncloa, sin embargo, arranca el curso a la defensiva: la crisis de Ceuta ha desplazado la agenda y ha tensado a los socios de los que dependen el decreto de vivienda y las cuentas. Este martes, el Consejo de Ministros aprobará la desclasificación de los informes sobre la crisis, que se harán públicos el miércoles.

articles.headline: Peinado cita a Begoña Gómez este martes a la audiencia previa al juicio con jurado popular
articles.subtitle: El juez convoca a las 18.00 a la esposa de Sánchez y a su asesora Cristina Álvarez, acusadas de tráfico de influencias y malversación, y rechaza aplazar la vista y el testigo que pedía la defensa. Quiere abrir el juicio oral antes de jubilarse el 27.
articles.body:
El juez Juan Carlos Peinado ha citado para este martes a las 18.00 la audiencia preliminar del juicio con jurado popular contra Begoña Gómez, esposa del presidente del Gobierno, y su asesora Cristina Álvarez, acusadas de tráfico de influencias y malversación. La vista se celebrará en los juzgados de Plaza de Castilla y las acusadas deben comparecer personalmente.

Es el trámite previo a la apertura del juicio oral, que el instructor quiere dictar antes de jubilarse el próximo 27 de septiembre. En el auto, Peinado rechazó la petición de la defensa de aplazar la vista y de interrogar como testigo a José Manuel Ruano, codirector de la cátedra que Gómez dirigió en la Universidad Complutense.

Tanto las defensas como la Fiscalía piden la absolución de las dos acusadas. La acusación popular que lidera Hazte Oír reclama 13 años de cárcel para Gómez y seis para Álvarez por malversación. La Audiencia de Madrid confirmó en julio el juicio con jurado y retiró los cargos de apropiación indebida del software y de corrupción en los negocios.

articles.headline: El Gobierno estrena su portal de vivienda pública con 800 pisos, ninguno en Madrid, Barcelona o Sevilla
articles.subtitle: Casa 47 abre siete convocatorias hasta el 21 de septiembre lejos de las grandes ciudades, con alquileres desde 350 euros y contratos prorrogables hasta 75 años. Sánchez admite que el mercado está "roto" y anuncia 1.500 pisos más.
articles.body:
El Gobierno presentó este lunes el portal digital de Casa 47, la entidad estatal de vivienda, que arranca con 800 pisos de alquiler asequible. La primera hornada se reparte por Alicante, Castellón, Valencia, Cataluña, Galicia, Navarra y Asturias: ninguno de los inmuebles está en Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia o Sevilla, y la mayor convocatoria en una gran ciudad es la de Gijón, con 18 viviendas.

Los requisitos combinan ingresos y precio: la renta no puede superar el 30% de los ingresos de la unidad de convivencia, que debe moverse entre 2 y 7,5 veces el IPREM, y los alquileres van de los 350 euros de una habitación a más de 1.000. Los contratos duran 14 años y pueden prorrogarse hasta 75, y la adjudicación se decide por sorteo ante notario.

Sánchez, que admitió que el mercado inmobiliario está "roto" y "desbocado", prometió que el parque "estará protegido para siempre" y que "muy pronto" se sumarán 1.500 viviendas más, con nuevas convocatorias cada trimestre. El portal centraliza el patrimonio de la antigua Sareb: más de 40.000 viviendas y 2.500 suelos.

articles.headline: Stormont reconvenes with clash over Drumcree as Orange Order files new parade application
articles.subtitle: MLAs clashed on the Assembly's first day back after recess. The First Minister says the issue is closed, unionists want the Parades Commission sacked, and a new 'limited' parade is planned for September 27.
articles.body:
The Assembly's first sitting after the summer recess opened with the Drumcree dispute, the first chance for MLAs to put on record their views since the High Court last month quashed the Parades Commission's determination on the annual Portadown parade.

TUV MLA Timothy Gaston urged the Secretary of State to remove the five remaining commissioners, saying the ruling had exposed "serious failings" and that the unionist community had no confidence left in the body. DUP MLA Jonathan Buckley called the commissioners' positions "untenable" and accused Sinn Féin of switching its position over mediation with the Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents. Sinn Féin's John O'Dowd, who represents Upper Bann, accused unionists of "reopening old wounds" and read out the names of those who died during the 1990s stand-offs, including Robert Hamill, kicked to death in Portadown, and the three Quinn brothers, aged between nine and eleven, who were burned to death in an arson attack.

Outside the chamber, First Minister Michelle O'Neill said the issue was "closed", describing the Orange Order's renewed application for a "limited" parade as "a direct provocation" on a community that had been settled for 28 years. The commission has blocked the route since 1998 and must now rule on the fresh application, which would see 60 order members walk from Drumcree Church on Sunday 27 September.

Alliance's Eóin Tennyson likened the row to "picking a scab with a chainsaw", while UUP deputy leader Diana Armstrong warned that a decision taken by the current membership risked "another court case within months". Commissioner Billy Gamble resigned last month after the quashed ruling, but chairwoman Evelyn Collins has refused to stand down.

articles.headline: Parties say Westminster's Stormont budget offer 'falls well short' after Bryant's first visit
articles.subtitle: The UK government is reported to have offered about £350m a year for three years to break the deadlock, still leaving an estimated £100m shortfall. Michelle O'Neill said she would 'hardball' the Secretary of State.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant made his first visit to Stormont on Monday in a bid to break the budget deadlock that has left the Executive unable to agree a budget for the current financial year.

Parties emerged saying the financial offer on the table "falls well short". DUP leader Gavin Robinson said it did not even deal with the pressures facing a single department: "Anybody who stands before you today and says look, we just need to get on and agree and accept something which will not get the job done, can explain to you the cuts that will come as a consequence, the redundancies that will come as a consequence, the consequence of unfunded transformation."

The additional cash is reported to be in the region of £350m a year over the next three years, which could still leave a shortfall of £100m a year. First Minister Michelle O'Neill said she would continue to "hardball" for a fairer funding settlement: "We're very much focused on getting a budget, but it needs to be the right budget. It needs to be a budget that reflects the needs of people here."

Health and education face significant shortfalls, and without an agreed budget departments may spend 95 per cent of last year's funding. Mr Bryant is expected to seek revenue-raising ideas such as water charges in return for extra cash. The SDLP's Claire Hanna said financial reforms could be examined in tandem with the talks but should not become a precondition for progress, and Alliance said the discussions were at an early stage and "a long way" from completion. Mr Bryant is also holding separate talks on reforming the Stormont institutions, a longer-term project likely to outlast next May's Assembly election; Taoiseach Micheál Martin said the proposals "need to be grasped".

articles.headline: Derry's St Columb's Hall returns to community ownership after £3.75m lottery award
articles.subtitle: The Grade A listed 'People's Hall', built in 1886 with public donations, has been bought by the St Columb's Hall Trust with National Lottery Heritage Fund money, unlocking a restoration of the whole building.
articles.body:
One of Derry's most historic buildings has returned to community ownership after the St Columb's Hall Trust completed its purchase of the Grade A listed landmark with £3.75m from the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

Construction of the hall, known to many as "the People's Hall", began in 1886 and was funded mainly by donations from local people before it opened its doors in 1888. It became one of the city's most important venues, hosting everyone from Roy Orbison to suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst, who spoke there in 1910, and Éamon de Valera, who rallied support for the cause of Irish independence in 1924. More recently, Channel 4's Derry Girls filmed some of its most famous Season 3 scenes in the building, which stopped hosting events in 2020. Around two-thirds of the hall is currently unusable.

The trust will fully restore the building and open it to the public, with work beginning in spring 2027: repairs and modernisation, a new rooftop terrace, a ground-floor exhibition area, a debate space and a creative entrepreneurial space.

Anne-Marie Gallagher from the trust said it had been "a long road": "St Columb's Hall is the embodiment of the spirit of our city... we want to keep building on that." Stella Byrne of the National Lottery Heritage Fund said the hall was being "sustainably redeveloped so that new generations and new audiences can freely access it".

The purchase is the latest in efforts to revive Derry's built heritage, alongside plans for the former Austins department store.

articles.headline: Russia resumes strikes on Kyiv as three-day pause for US envoys' visit comes to an end
articles.subtitle: Explosions were heard over the Ukrainian capital early on Tuesday, hours after the halt Vladimir Putin ordered during Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner's peace push expired. Poland scrambled aviation and Ukraine struck back in Saratov.
articles.body:
Russia struck Kyiv early on Tuesday, hours after the three-day pause ordered by Vladimir Putin during the visit of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner came to an end. Explosions were heard over the Ukrainian capital as Ukraine's air force warned of fast jet-powered drones approaching from several directions, and Kyiv's military administration reported at least two people killed and seven wounded.

The State Emergency Service said drones hit the Boryspil and Fastiv districts on the outskirts of the capital, where fires broke out at an industrial site and a logistics complex was hit twice. Air raid alerts for the wider Kyiv region lasted for hours, and neighbouring Poland, a Nato member, scrambled military aviation to protect its airspace.

The pause, which both Moscow and Kyiv observed for their capitals, had raised hopes that the envoys' talks could revive the stalled negotiations, with the Kremlin saying the window for diplomacy was "not limitless". Russian state media said the halt expired on Monday evening and Moscow saw no need to extend it. Attacks on other regions continued even during the pause.

Ukraine also struck back: the governor of Russia's Saratov region said a Ukrainian drone attack hit civilian infrastructure and injured several people. Neither side has signalled a return to the negotiating table, and the strikes came as President Volodymyr Zelensky repeated that Ukraine needed more air defences before winter.

articles.headline: Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect as Trump threatens to stop Bombardier selling jets in the US
articles.subtitle: Duties of 15 to 50 per cent on almost $20bn of US goods kicked in at midnight, hours after Donald Trump said the Quebec planemaker must build in America. Ottawa unveiled a C$5.42bn support package.
articles.body:
Canada's retaliatory tariffs on nearly $20bn of US imports took effect at midnight on Tuesday, matching Washington's levies "dollar for dollar" and escalating the trade war between the two neighbours. The duties, ranging from 15 to 50 per cent, cover steel, household appliances, agricultural equipment and dairy products - more than 700 lines in total.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a C$5.42bn support package for affected small businesses and workers, and the Kiel Institute estimates that US importers and consumers absorb about 96 per cent of the tariff burden across some 550 consumer goods.

Hours before the duties landed, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that "there will be NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!!!", saying the Canadian planemaker could only sell in America if it built there. Bombardier, based in Montreal, employs about 3,500 workers in Kansas and says its Challenger and Global jets are fully compliant with the US-Mexico-Canada trade deal. Quebec premier Christine Fréchette called the company "a flagship of our economy" and said Quebec would not be dictated to over where its companies must produce.

Negotiations collapsed late last month, and the dispute has spilled beyond trade: Washington has also signed an order renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America" for official federal use, deepening the sense of crisis between the two allies.

articles.headline: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon kill at least 13 in the worst escalation since the June ceasefire
articles.subtitle: Lebanese officials said children were among those killed as jets hit Kfar Rumman, Rihan and Nabatieh, and President Joseph Aoun called the raids a 'dangerous escalation' that could unravel the truce with Hezbollah.
articles.body:
Israeli air strikes across southern Lebanon on Monday killed at least 13 people, including women and children, according to Lebanon's health ministry - the bloodiest escalation since the June ceasefire ended the war between Israel and Hezbollah.

Most of the victims died in Kfar Rumman, where an overnight strike destroyed a three-storey residential building as families slept. Rescuers counted 11 bodies in the rubble, two of them children, alongside four women, and an 18-year-old rescuer was killed in a second strike on the same town. One more person was killed in nearby Rihan and nine people were wounded in Nabatieh. AFP photographers at the scene saw school books scattered through the debris. Early reports from other agencies put the overall toll at 11 or 12 before the health ministry's final count.

Israel said it had struck Hezbollah infrastructure in response to two explosive drones launched towards its troops near the border, and that it had killed a Hezbollah member near Beaufort Castle. It insisted it remained "committed to the ceasefire agreement". Hezbollah has not yet commented.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun called the attacks a "dangerous escalation" that jeopardised the US-brokered truce. Violence has been creeping upward since Israel said on Thursday it had seized the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge. Beirut says more than 4,300 people have been killed in Lebanon since the conflict began in March.

articles.headline: Thousands gather in Belgrade for the funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladic as the EU denounces his glorification
articles.subtitle: The convicted 'Butcher of Bosnia', who died aged 84 while serving a life sentence for the Srebrenica genocide, was buried with military honours after a service led by the Serbian Orthodox patriarch.
articles.body:
Thousands of people gathered in Belgrade on Monday for the funeral of Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb commander convicted of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, who died aged 84 in a Dutch prison hospital while serving a life sentence imposed by the UN tribunal in The Hague.

His coffin, draped in the Serbian flag, was flown home on a government plane and buried with military honours at the capital's Alley of the Greats cemetery. The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, and attended by Serbia's defence and justice ministers, while free buses brought mourners from across Serbia and Bosnia and Red Star Belgrade fans had unveiled a Mladic tifo before Sunday's derby.

The European Union condemned the scenes, saying: "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries." Serbia, an EU candidate, had earlier dropped plans for a full state funeral after objections from European leaders.

For the families of Mladic's victims, the spectacle reopened old wounds: during the Bosnian war, Mladic's forces killed more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica and besieged Sarajevo for four years, and Monday's crowds included people who remembered him only as the man responsible.

articles.headline: Eiffel Tower shut as staff strike over women being moved for a Hindu delegation's visit
articles.subtitle: Workers walked out after female employees were asked to leave their posts when a BAPS group of around 100 people visited the monument on Saturday. The operator admitted the conditions 'should not have been accepted'.
articles.body:
The Eiffel Tower was closed to visitors on Monday after staff went on strike over an incident on Saturday, when female workers were asked to leave their positions so that men from a visiting Hindu religious delegation could take their place.

Around 100 people linked to the BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha, whose leader Praghat Swami is in France ahead of the consecration of the movement's first major temple near Paris, had arranged a visit to the monument. Union representative Diane Davoine said women staff were "humiliated" and told to move as the delegation arrived. SETE, the company that operates the tower, said the group had asked to limit "interactions with women" during the visit and admitted "these conditions should not have been accepted... they are not in line with SETE's values".

Paris mayor Emmanuel Grégoire promised an investigation and called the workers' anger "legitimate", while politicians from across the spectrum weighed in: Marine Le Pen said France would "never accept that the presence of women be limited", and presidential hopeful Gabriel Attal insisted that no culture or belief could dictate to women their place. The BAPS group in Paris said the visit had been "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team" and apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused".

The dispute is the latest flashpoint over religion and public space in France, where laicite - the strict separation of religion and state - remains a sensitive subject ahead of next year's presidential election.

articles.headline: Apple's 'Surprise and Shine' event preview: a first foldable iPhone and the iPhone 18 Pro land on Wednesday
articles.subtitle: Five years after Samsung's first foldable, Apple is expected to debut the book-style iPhone Ultra alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, with new CEO John Ternus hosting. Rumoured prices start at $2,000.
articles.body:
Apple's September event, named "Surprise and Shine", takes place on Wednesday at 10am Pacific time, and this year's gathering is one of the most anticipated in years: the company is expected to finally debut a foldable iPhone, more than five years after Samsung launched its first.

Rumoured to be called the iPhone Ultra, it is a book-style device with a 5.5-inch cover display that opens into a 7.8-inch inner screen, essentially an iPad mini that folds in half. To keep the device thin - around 4.5mm when unfolded - Apple is reported to have dropped Face ID in favour of a Touch ID button on the side and to have skipped a telephoto camera. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says early testers found it premium-feeling, with a minimal crease and a durable liquid-metal hinge, plus MagSafe support. Prices are expected to start around $2,000 and could reach $2,500.

It will also be the first Apple event hosted by John Ternus, the company's new CEO, who took over from Tim Cook, now executive chairman. Alongside the foldable, Apple is expected to announce the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max with a 2nm A20 Pro chip and a variable-aperture camera system; there is no standard iPhone 18 this year, with reports pointing to a spring 2027 release. Apple Watch Series 12, AirPods 5 and possibly a new Home Hub are also tipped, and the event should confirm iOS 27's release dates.

Memory costs hang over the whole lineup: component prices driven up by the global RAM shortage have reportedly pushed the Pro models up by $100-$300, and pre-orders, originally expected on Friday, may slip to Saturday because of the date's 9/11 symbolism, with deliveries beginning around 18 September.

articles.headline: 'RAMageddon': soaring memory prices are about to hit your next phone, laptop and console
articles.subtitle: Counterpoint says the DRAM inside a 16GB phone cost about $42 in mid-2025 and $181 a year later, and prices could take years to settle. Apple, Samsung and Google are all passing the costs on.
articles.body:
Call it "chipflation" or "RAMageddon": the memory shortage is reversing decades of falling component prices and pushing up the cost of almost every new device. Counterpoint Research says smartphone DRAM prices rose about 56 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 and around 83 per cent in the second - the 16 gigabytes of DRAM in a modern phone cost roughly $42 in mid-2025 and $181 a year later.

The squeeze, amplified by AI's seemingly unending appetite for memory, took shape before the AI boom even peaked: suppliers shifted production towards lucrative data-centre chips, and new fabrication plants take years to come online. "Memory prices" appeared in 473 company earnings calls last quarter, according to AlphaSense, as executives from every corner of consumer electronics warned of rising bills.

Apple is the most visible test case. Tim Cook has described memory pricing as a "100-year flood", and the company has already raised prices on Macs, iPads, HomePods and the Vision Pro. The Wall Street Journal calculates, using TechInsights estimates, that the iPhone 18 Pro could start at $1,299 - $200 more than the iPhone 17 Pro - though Apple's decision to delay the standard iPhone 18 until spring 2027 leaves its near-term lineup at the high-margin end of the market.

Samsung and Google have each raised the starting prices of their flagships by $100 this year, and game consoles, laptops and Steam Decks have all crept up. Analysts expect the annual increases to slow to single or low double digits, but component prices are expected to settle at least three times higher than before the crisis.

articles.headline: Victim loses £250,000 to fraudsters using an AI-generated video of a 'well-known' financial personality
articles.subtitle: PSNI says the Co Down victim was duped by a deepfake advertisement promising investment returns, then persuaded to borrow money and hand over remote access to a computer. Police warn no endorsement is proof of legitimacy.
articles.body:
A person in Northern Ireland has lost £250,000 (around €291,000) to a "sophisticated and substantial" investment fraud built on an AI-generated video, police have warned.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland said the victim, in the Ards and North Down area, first saw what appeared to be an AI-generated video of a well-known personality from the financial sector promoting an investment opportunity and claiming significant returns. The PSNI did not confirm whose likeness was used, but BBC News NI said scams circulating online have featured financial experts such as Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett.

After an initial small investment, the victim was contacted through WhatsApp and encouraged to make further payments. The fraudsters then persuaded them to create multiple online accounts and to grant remote access to a computer, claiming they were helping with the investment, before encouraging the victim to borrow money to keep investing. Funds were transferred to accounts controlled by the criminals.

Superintendent Joanne Gibson, chair of the Scamwise Partnership, said fraudsters could create "extremely convincing" advertisements, websites and communications: "The use of artificial intelligence means that videos, voices and apparent endorsements from recognisable people can also be fabricated." Inspector Youle, who investigated the case, urged the public to be cautious if contacted through messaging services and encouraged to transfer money, open additional accounts, borrow to invest, allow remote access to a computer, or make further payments to release an investment. Police advise independently verifying who you are dealing with and checking that anyone offering financial services is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.
